extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, scholars, and writers interested in F. Scott Fitzgerald and Jazz Age literature
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic biography of F. Scott Fitzgerald that summarizes his life, major works, themes, stylistic traits, publishing practices, and critical reception; useful for readers and writers studying his technique and the Jazz Age. Not a how-to manual but contains repeated descriptive statements that imply standards for evaluating or emulating his writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting the Jazz Age (flamboyance and excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald is best known for his novels depicting the flamboyance and excess of the Jazz Age, a term he popularized; his work captures the era's giddiness, moral permissiveness, and obsession with self-gratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke the Jazz Age, foreground rituals of wealth, parties, consumerism, and social spectacle (e.g., lavish Long Island parties, Biltmore/Commodore hotel episodes). Use social detail and atmosphere to dramatize cultural permissiveness and the emotional costs of excess; avoid flattening the era into mere glamour—show its moral disquiet and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic tone: romantic yet cynical; lyrical and astringent
rubrics_metrics.description: "Romantic, but also cynical; he is bitter as well as ecstatic; astringent as well as lyrical... he has the Irish gift for turning language into something iridescent and surprising." (Edmund Wilson's description of Fitzgerald's style.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a mix of lyricism and ironic distance: combine romantic description with sharp satire, quick wit, and unexpected turns of phrase. Use language that can be both beautiful and mocking; cultivate cadences that surprise the reader rather than rely on flat realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful, intricately patterned composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald described plans for works 'beautiful and intricately patterned' (his conception for The Great Gatsby); critics note carefully crafted structure and patterning in his major novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work toward structural coherence and carefully arranged motifs and echoes across the text. Be willing to discard false starts and revise extensively to achieve an integrated pattern; attention to recurring images and formal symmetry is important for an enduring novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization drawn from real life (use of models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald often modeled characters on real acquaintances (e.g., Ginevra King as a model for Daisy, Max Gerlach inspiring Gatsby, Zelda influencing characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-life personalities and incidents as raw material for fictional characters, transforming and fictionalizing details to serve theme and narrative. Beware of ethical and marital fallout (as happened in Fitzgerald's life) and of over-literal transposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting for magazine salability: authenticity then plot twist
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald 'would first write his stories in an 'authentic' manner, then rewrite them to add plot twists which increased their salability as magazine stories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for commercial magazines, produce an authentic draft focused on voice and character, then revise to add clear plot hooks or twists that increase immediate reader interest and marketability. Be aware critics (and peers like Hemingway) might disparage such tailoring as 'whoring', so balance craft and commerce consciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring thematic focus: wealth, class, and the unfairness of love
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring theme in Fitzgerald's work is the interplay of wealth and desire—e.g., 'the whole idea of Gatsby' is 'the unfairness of a poor young man not being able to marry a girl with money.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center narratives on tensions between class and personal longing; dramatize how economic status shapes relationships, aspirations, and moral outcomes. Reuse and rework core thematic concerns across stories and novels to build a coherent authorial preoccupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with narrative structure (risking contemporary confusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tender Is the Night's unconventional structure 'threw off many critics who felt Fitzgerald had not lived up to their expectations'—experimentation may challenge readers even if reputation grows later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shy away from nontraditional structures or rearranged chronology, but expect mixed immediate reception; weigh the artistic payoff of formal experimentation against potential reader confusion and critical misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing artistic ambition with commercial necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald alternated between striving for high-art novels and writing lucrative short stories for magazines to maintain finances; he sometimes compromised artistic priorities for income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the economic realities of writing: you may need to produce market-oriented pieces alongside longer artistic projects. Strategize time and revisions to keep both streams viable—e.g., reserve long-form revision time while using shorter, saleable pieces to fund living costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid social milieu and scene to reveal character and theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald frequently uses party scenes, hotels, beaches, and the social play of the era (e.g., Long Island mansions, Riviera casinos) to reflect moral states and interpersonal dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage scenes in socially charged settings that both dazzle and expose character vulnerabilities. Sensory detail and social rituals can be leveraged to dramatize characters' inner lives and the moral texture of a period; avoid merely ornamental description—make setting work thematically.
